new_statements.quote: The general character of the pronunciation is dental and nasal; the sounds are formed principally in the fore part of the mouth, and the intonations are varied and pleasing. The accent, in words of two syllables, is usually on the first, and in words of three or more on the antepenultimate; but to this there are many exceptions.

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record for Awabakal has an empty rule; Hale supplies a placement (initial in disyllables, antepenult in longer words), which is compatible with Threlkeld 1834's initial accent for two- and three-syllable words but is a general statement about Australian languages, derived from Threlkeld and Watson, not an independent description of Awabakal.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Disyllables: accent on the first syllable; words of three or more syllables: accent on the antepenult (which is the initial syllable in trisyllables); many exceptions. Stated for 'the Australian dialects' Hale observed, i.e. Threlkeld's Lake Macquarie language (which Hale calls 'Kamilarai') and Watson's Wiradurei, not for Awabakal alone.
new_statements.exceptions: 'to this there are many exceptions' (none listed in the phonology section); in the Kamilarai grammar (p. 485, from Threlkeld) nouns in -ro 'require the accent to be shifted to the o' in the active nominative (mákoro, fish; active nominative makaró).
new_statements.identity_note: Threlkeld 1834 describes 'the language as spoken by the Aborigines in the vicinity of Hunter's River, Lake Macquarie', the variety now called Awabakal (the name 'Awabakal' is not used in the 1834 grammar). Hale 1846 presents the same Lake Macquarie language under the name 'Kamilarai', which he says is the name given to it by the Wellington Valley (Wiradurei) people (p. 482); this is not the Gamilaraay of the Namoi region. Hale's accent statement (p. 483) is framed for 'the Australian dialects' generally, based on this language and Wiradurei.

new_statements.quote: [p. 2] The language requires but one marked accent, which serves for the prolongation of the syllable; as, bón, him; bún, the root of to smite. [p. 4] In general dissyllables and trisyllables accent the first syllable; as, Pún-ti-mai, a messenger; Pír-ri-wul, a chief, king, &c. Compound derivative words, being descriptive nouns, have the accent universally on the last syllable; as, Wi-yel-li-kán, one who speaks [...] Verbs in the present and past tenses have their accent on the particles denoting such tense: as, Ta-tán, eats. Wi-yán, speaks. [...] In the future tenses the accent is always on the last syllable but one [...] [p. 5] Thus, two accents are apparent. One the Radical accent. The other the shifting one which belongs to the particles.

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record for Awabakal has no rule; Threlkeld is the primary source and gives initial accent for simple two- and three-syllable words plus suffix-governed shifting accent in derived and inflected forms. Compatible with Hale 1846 for two- and three-syllable words.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Simple words of two and three syllables carry the accent on the first syllable (the 'Radical accent'); a second, 'shifting' accent belongs to the suffixed particles: agentive/descriptive derivatives in -kán, -ngéil take final accent, present/past tense particles are accented (Ta-tán, Wi-yán), future tenses are accented on the penult (Bún-kil-li-nun), present participles on the final (Bún-kil-lín), past participles on the penult (Bún-kil-li-á-la), the state participle -tó-a-ra on the antepenult; nouns in -ro shift the accent to the final -ó in the readers case (Ma-ko-ró, p. 18). Threlkeld's single accent mark also 'serves for the prolongation of the syllable', so his accent conflates vowel length with prominence (bun 'accidental' vs bún 'smite').
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not as such; Threlkeld distinguishes a 'Radical accent' on the root and a 'shifting' accent on the particles (p. 5), i.e. two accents can be apparent in one word (e.g. Bún-tó-a-ra). 'Emphasis' (p. 5) is pragmatic: extra stress on the particles, or on the last syllable (often changed to -oú) when attention is commanded, or on the particle of agency (Ngá-tó-a 'It is I').
new_statements.exceptions: Derived and inflected words: descriptive derivatives accent the last syllable; tense particles attract the accent; future = penult; participles as listed; -ro nouns shift accent to final -ó as readers; the accent also distinguishes wish from affirmation (Kau-wa 'be it so' vs Kau-wá 'so it is').
new_statements.identity_note: Threlkeld 1834 describes 'the language as spoken by the Aborigines in the vicinity of Hunter's River, Lake Macquarie', the variety now called Awabakal (the name 'Awabakal' is not used in the 1834 grammar). Hale 1846 presents the same Lake Macquarie language under the name 'Kamilarai', which he says is the name given to it by the Wellington Valley (Wiradurei) people (p. 482); this is not the Gamilaraay of the Namoi region. Hale's accent statement (p. 483) is framed for 'the Australian dialects' generally, based on this language and Wiradurei.

readall_conflicts: Threlkeld 1834 (the primary description) and Hale 1846 (derived from Threlkeld and Watson) agree that two- and three-syllable words are accented on the first syllable. They part on longer words: Hale generalises to the antepenult 'with many exceptions', whereas Threlkeld gives suffix-governed placements (final accent in -kán derivatives and present participles, penult in futures and past participles, antepenult in -tó-a-ra state participles, final -ó in the readers case of -ro nouns), so Hale's antepenult rule matches only some of Threlkeld's derived forms. A further caveat: Threlkeld's single accent mark 'serves for the prolongation of the syllable' (p. 2), so his 'accent' partly marks vowel length rather than stress, and no modern phonetic source was in the list to settle it. Two listed works (Threlkeld 1858 and 1827) could not be opened.
